questions.question: Let $S=\{a,b,c,d\}$. Is $\{\{a\},\{b,c\},\{d\}\}$ a partition?
options: No, because the pieces must all have the same number of elements
Yes, because a partition only needs its pieces to cover $S$
Yes, the pieces are nonempty, disjoint and cover $S$
No, because singletons like $\{a\}$ cannot be pieces

questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. Which collection is a partition?
options: $\{\varnothing,S\}$

questions.question: A survey uses age groups under $30$, $30$ to $60$, and $60$ or older. What boundary issue must be avoided for a partition?
options: Every group must have the same number of respondents
Ages $30$ and $60$ must be left out of every group
A respondent aged exactly $60$ must not fall into two groups
The three groups must be independent events for each respondent

questions.question: Which conditions together define a partition $\{B_i\colon i\in I\}$ of a set $E$?
options: Blocks nonempty and pairwise disjoint, union contained in $E$
Blocks nonempty, union equal to $E$
Blocks pairwise disjoint, union equal to $E$
Blocks nonempty and pairwise disjoint, union equal to $E$

questions.question: Let $B_1,B_2,B_3$ be a partition of the sample space $S$ and let $A$ be any event. Which statement about $A\cap B_1$, $A\cap B_2$, $A\cap B_3$ is always true?
options: They are disjoint and their union is $A$
They are disjoint and their union is $S$
They are nonempty, so they form a partition of $A$
Their union is $A$, but two of them may overlap

questions.question: Each of the shipping methods standard, express and pickup is used by at least one order. When do these three methods partition the set of orders?
options: When each order uses at least one of the methods
When each order uses exactly one of the methods
When each order uses at most one of the methods
When each method is used by the same number of orders

questions.question: Let $A$ be an event in a sample space $S$. Which condition is necessary and sufficient for $\{A,A^c\}$ to be a partition of $S$ into two blocks?
options: $A\ne\varnothing$ and $A^c\ne\varnothing$
$\mathbb{P}(A)>0$ and $\mathbb{P}(A^c)>0$
$A\cap A^c=\varnothing$
$\mathbb{P}(A)=\mathbb{P}(A^c)=\tfrac{1}{2}$

questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4\}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\{1\})=0.2$, $\mathbb{P}(\{2\})=0.3$, $\mathbb{P}(\{3\})=0.5$ and $\mathbb{P}(\{4\})=0$. Is $\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\}\}$ a partition of $S$?
options: Yes, since the blocks are disjoint and their probabilities sum to $1$
No, since $4$ lies in no block; adding the block $\{4\}$ gives a partition
No, and adding $\{4\}$ would not help, since a block cannot have probability $0$
No, since the blocks would need equal probabilities, unlike $0.2$, $0.3$, $0.5$

questions.question: A fair die is rolled, $B_1=\{1,2,3\}$, $B_2=\{3,4,5,6\}$ and $A=\{1,3,5\}$. What is $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_1)+\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_2)$?
